newsitem.title: USA: Calif. seen ending fiscal year without reserve.
newsitem.headline: Calif. seen ending fiscal year without reserve.

text.p: California's Legislative Analyst projected Thursday that the state would end the current fiscal year with virtually no reserve and incur a budget deficit of almost $1 billion by the end of fiscal 1998-99 unless corrective action was taken.

The Legislative Analyst's office, which provides analysis and nonpartisan advice to the Legislature on fiscal and policy issues, said in a report that the state would end fiscal 1996-97 with an $8 million reserve, much less than the budget reserve estimate of $305 million.
The primary reason for the change in the reserve was the underaccounting of school enrollment, Legislative Analyst Elizabeth Hill told reporters at a press briefing in Sacramento.
The state's fiscal condition has improved markedly over the past three years, with the general fund moving from a substantial deficit into rough fiscal balance.
Hill's projections for 1996-97 through 1998-99 indicated budget shortfalls would re-emerge without legislative action.
"The legislators and the governor are in a trade-off period in preparing the state for the future," Hill said.

"The Legislature should budget by priority and not by formula," she said, referring to state Proposition 98. Under Proposition 98, education spending will increase rapidly in the coming years, putting pressure on the state's general fund budget, Hill said.
"It is time to unlock the budget to allow the Legislature and the governor to run the state," Hill said.

Hill said expenditure growth would exceed revenue growth during the next three years. This should result in a declining operating surplus in 1996-97 and increasingly large deficits, reaching about $1 billion in 1998-99, she said.
The Department of Finance said the Legislative Analyst's figures were baseline forecasts that assumed the governor and Legislature would make no changes to growth in state spending.

"That's not going to happen," said H.D. Palmer, a spokesman for the governor's Department of Finance. "The governor will present a budget in January for yet another year of the state living within its means."
The Legislature was not scheduled to reconvene until December 2. The governor will submit his 1997-98 budget proposal to lawmakers in early January.
Hill said the projected five-year capital outlay needs for the state totaled almost $39 billion. Education, transportation and corrections will need the most funding.
In recent years, the vast majority of capital outlay has been financed with state bonds. The major exception is transportation, which is financed primarily from state special funds and federal funds.
Hill said the state would continue to outpace the nation in economic growth over the next three years. She said state revenues should grow at an annual average rate of 5.4 percent through 1998-99.
She estimated that personal income growth would peak at 7.4 percent this year.
